notes: llama.cpp cannot batch an LFM3-d1 decision: its decision graph reads the whole prompt as one flat token run (src/models/lfm3.cpp, build_attn_inp_no_cache) and the recurrent layers' short convolutions would mix the sequences, so the server refuses to put two decision requests in one ubatch (tools/server/server-context.cpp: task.decision.no_batching, set unconditionally for this model family, with upstream's own TODO describing what this server does) and a tick of 64 characters x 3 questions is 192 separate prefills, each streaming the 1.76 GB of Q8_0 weights out of memory. This server runs the same arithmetic as llama.cpp - the same norms, sandwich norms, short convolutions, NeoX rotary, grouped-query attention and head gate, the same non-causal dense attention and causal sliding-window attention, the same output head, the same label groups, the same temperature and the same decision head - and adds the two things the flat decision graph lacks: a block-diagonal attention mask, so a dense layer of one sequence never sees another sequence and a sliding-window layer sees only its own sequence's last 256 positions, and a per-sequence short convolution, so the recurrent layers' six-token window never crosses from one sequence into the next. The batch is right-padded to the longest prompt, which is safe because the convolutions look backwards and the attention masks the padded keys out, so a batched forward pass is numerically the same as running each prompt on its own (tests/test_batching_exactness.py checks that against an independent numpy reference written from llama.cpp's graph). A single worker thread drains the request queue into batches, so one tick of 192 questions becomes a handful of forward passes and the weights are streamed once per batch instead of once per decision. The engine moves the activations as few times as it can: the rotary is written as one complex multiplication (the rotation of a pair is the product of the complex numbers x0+i*x1 and cos+i*sin) instead of ten passes over the head, the short convolution runs in fp16 with cuDNN's fp32 accumulator instead of copying its input into fp32, the shared key and value heads are read by the attention instead of being repeated, and a tick's sequences are run in chunks of 32 to keep the GPU's peak down - together 1.64x the engine it started with, and the answers are unchanged. The server speaks llama.cpp's wire (the same POST /v1/systemone body and answer shape), so the answers are llama.cpp's answers: the two servers agree on 99.09% of the 768 questions, and all 7 of the disagreements are questions where the two leading options are within 0.4% of each other. The cause is the precision of the activations: llama.cpp's matmuls go through the MMQ path, which quantises the activations to eight bits, while this server keeps them in fp16, so on a question whose two leading options are level the two engines pick different ones. llama.cpp's own answers do not move between runs (0 changes over the same 768 questions asked twice, results/baseline_self_stability.json), so these are a real numerical difference rather than its noise. The box is shared and its load moves by a factor of two within a run, so the numbers are the median over 15 interleaved rounds - the baseline, then ours, then the baseline, then ours, so that the drift hits both of them the same way - and every round's number is in results/rounds/pooled.json.
